name: Ketoconazole
lead: Ketoconazole is a synthetic imidazole antifungal. It is available as oral tablets for serious fungal infections and as topical creams, foams and shampoos (such as Nizoral) for skin and scalp conditions including dandruff, seborrheic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor [1][2][3].

In hair-loss communities, ketoconazole 2% shampoo is discussed as an adjunct to finasteride and minoxidil, on the theory that it may reduce scalp inflammation and local androgen activity. A 2020 systematic review of topical ketoconazole in androgenetic alopecia (AGA) called it a promising adjunctive treatment, based on five human studies (318 participants) and two animal studies [4]. The US shampoo label lists dandruff-type and tinea versicolor indications, not hair loss [2].

Oral ketoconazole carries an FDA boxed warning for liver toxicity and other risks, whereas the shampoo is applied topically and is not detected in plasma after chronic scalp use according to its label [1][2].

paras: Oral ketoconazole was developed in the 1970s and first approved by the FDA in 1981 as an early broad-spectrum oral antifungal for severe systemic mycoses [1]. Topical forms treat dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, which involve Malassezia yeasts and which reviews list ketoconazole among recommended topical options for [3]. The US shampoo label is indicated for pityriasis (tinea) versicolor [2]. Earlier trials examined it for pityriasis versicolor and compared antifungal preparations for anti-inflammatory activity [5][6].

People with pattern hair loss use ketoconazole shampoo alongside standard treatments. A 2024 systematic review of AGA management found that many treatments promote hair growth and favoured a multifaceted, individualised approach [7].

The 2020 systematic review of topical ketoconazole in AGA included seven articles: two animal studies and five human studies with 318 participants in total. Murine studies reported more hair regrowth than controls; human studies reported increased hair shaft diameter, and one reported a significant rise in pilary index, with improvement on photographic and subjective assessment [4]. The authors described it as a promising adjunct, rather than a first-line treatment [4].
Evidence comparing it directly with finasteride or minoxidil in large randomised trials was not identified in the sources reviewed.

In 11 double-blind trials of the shampoo in 264 patients with dandruff or seborrheic dermatitis, increased hair loss and irritation occurred in under 1 percent; open-label safety studies reported abnormal hair texture, scalp pustules, dryness and itching, each once in 41 patients [2]. As with other shampoos, oily or dry hair and scalp have been reported [2].

Oral ketoconazole carries severe hepatotoxicity risk, estimated at about 1 in 2,000 to 15,000 users in a general reference, and in 2013 the FDA limited its oral use and added boxed warnings for liver injury, adrenal insufficiency and drug interactions through CYP3A4 inhibition [1]. The shampoo label gives a pregnancy category C and notes that the drug is not detected in plasma after chronic shampooing [2]. Ketoconazole has been studied as a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor affecting many other drugs [8].

In fungi, ketoconazole blocks ergosterol synthesis, a key component of cell membranes [1]. It also inhibits steroid hormone synthesis, which is why it has been used off-label in Cushing's syndrome and advanced prostate cancer [1]. The proposed mechanism in hair loss, discussed in forums, involves reduced scalp inflammation and antiandrogenic effects; reviews describe it as promising rather than established [4]. A pharmacokinetic study showed food impairs oral ketoconazole absorption [9].

On looksmax.org users recommend Nizoral for itchy scalp and dandruff, and some say hair shedding fell after starting it; a poster described a lifelong dandruff problem resolving and fewer hairs in the shower [10]. Other threads discuss dry skin and irritation from frequent use, shedding during early use, and long-term results combining finasteride, minoxidil and Nizoral [11][12][13]. Another thread asks whether it blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT, and one post proposes ketoconazole as an alternative to minoxidil, which it argues has hormonal drawbacks [14][15]. On T Nation members mention using it every other day as a proactive measure against thinning [16].

Topical ketoconazole in AGA has been summarised in a 2020 systematic review of five human studies (318 participants), which reported increased shaft diameter and some improvement in pilary index and photographs [4]. A 2024 systematic review of AGA management places it within a broader multifaceted approach [7]. For its labelled uses, a long-term safety study of ketoconazole 2% foam in seborrheic dermatitis enrolled 498 patients [17]. Studies of oral ketoconazole have mainly concerned fungal infection, drug interactions and endocrine uses [9][18].

timeline.event: Ketoconazole developed as an oral imidazole antifungal [1].
FDA limits oral use and adds boxed warnings [1].
Systematic review of topical ketoconazole in androgenetic alopecia [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, ketoconazole shampoo is described as a low-cost adjunct for hair retention, often added to finasteride and minoxidil routines, and as a dandruff fix [10][12][16].

claims.claim: Nizoral reduces shedding and may help male pattern baldness beyond treating dandruff.
claims.believers: Posters report fewer hairs in the shower after switching, and suggest a fungal component worsens pattern hair loss [10].
claims.experts: A systematic review reports increased shaft diameter in human studies and calls it a promising adjunct; the US shampoo label does not list hair loss as an indication [4][2].

claims.claim: Ketoconazole blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT.
claims.believers: Members ask whether it acts as an antiandrogen and propose it as a safer alternative to minoxidil [14][15].
claims.experts: Ketoconazole inhibits steroid hormone synthesis at systemic doses, and the shampoo label states it is not detected in plasma after chronic scalp use [1][2].

claims.claim: Early shedding after starting ketoconazole is normal.
claims.believers: A thread discusses hair shedding during early treatment [13].
claims.experts: The shampoo label reports increased normal hair loss in under 1 percent of patients in trials [2].

claims.claim: Frequent use can dry and irritate the scalp and skin.
claims.believers: A poster washing twice weekly for three months reported dry skin and irritation [11].
claims.experts: The label lists dryness, itching and abnormal hair texture among reported effects [2].

claims.claim: Ketoconazole shampoo is part of an effective finasteride, minoxidil and Nizoral routine.
claims.believers: A thread presents multi-year results with that combination [12].
claims.experts: A 2024 systematic review of AGA management favoured a multifaceted, individualised approach to treatment [7].

card.summary: Antifungal dandruff shampoo that hair-loss communities add to finasteride and minoxidil; small studies hint at benefit, large trials are missing.
card.note: Oral ketoconazole has a boxed warning for liver toxicity; the shampoo is the form used for hair.

quick.overview:
Ketoconazole is an antifungal. As a shampoo it treats dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, and many hair-loss forum members use it a couple of times a week as an add-on to finasteride and minoxidil.

A 2020 systematic review of five small human studies found increased hair shaft thickness and called it a promising adjunct. It has not been tested in large trials against standard treatments.
quick.mechanism: It blocks fungal cell-membrane synthesis, which reduces Malassezia yeast and scalp inflammation. Proposed antiandrogen effects on the scalp are discussed but not established.
quick.risks: The shampoo causes mild irritation, dryness or itching in a small share of users. Oral ketoconazole carries boxed warnings for liver injury and drug interactions and is restricted by the FDA.
